Lenape

Lenape histories connect an eastern homeland with distinct present communities and different displacement routes. This reading foundation includes community accounts, a primary treaty, language education and critical scholarship. Its Texas coverage is introductory and specifically scoped.

  • Current governments, homeland communities, citizenship and recognition require individually scoped contemporary evidence. One publisher’s position in identity disputes is not an Atlas-wide adjudication.
  • Moraviantown’s battle-outcome description and universal first-treaty assertion are not adopted. Undated population, land figures and legal claims are omitted.
  • Munsee and other language varieties, Canadian community histories, women’s histories, later land/government changes and wider Lenape-authored work remain unevenly covered.
  • Original archival records, treaty implementation, current legal instruments and books cited by the institutional histories remain unread. The scholarly article is a selected-page inspection.

These images have individual, documented connections to this entry. Their captions and source records define the people, place, object, and period shown; no one image represents every community within a broader label.

Bód-a-sin, Chief of the Tribe, 1830
George Catlin, 1830. Smithsonian American Art Museum, Gift of Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Jr., 1985.66.274. Public domain.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — SAAM item marked Free to use

Smithsonian American Art Museum explicitly identifies Bód-a-sin as a Delaware/Lenape chief. George Catlin’s 1830 oil portrait is an outside artist’s historical portrayal of one named person, not a documentary photograph, Lenape-made art, a generic Native likeness, or an image of a present government. The museum says it was probably painted at Fort Leavenworth in today’s Kansas; that uncertainty is retained. This image does not establish a Texas connection, exact territorial boundaries, current clothing or cultural practice, descent to a particular government, or community endorsement. No meanings are assigned to the sitter’s clothing or ornaments. The museum’s paired Delaware/Lenape identification supports these two overlapping directory reading labels. They do not count as two distinct nations or imply one present government. Complete 2461x3000 museum-delivered source JPEG inspected and preserved. Web copy resized proportionally to 1477x1800 and recompressed at quality 88; no pixel crop, added detail, generated material, retouching or recoloring. Directory cards and opened-page backgrounds may use disclosed CSS crops/overlays. Preserve a full-frame route where possible. CSS crops/overlays apply to cards and backgrounds; the opened image preserves the complete delivered source frame.

01

Names and distinct present communities

Lenape is broader than any one government. Delaware Nation’s history distinguishes its Anadarko community from Delaware Tribe of Indians and other Lenape governments. Similar names do not make these institutions interchangeable.

Read the sources [2] Delaware Nation

02

An eastern homeland and overlapping reading labels

The Tribe’s introduction locates Lenape history in the Delaware Valley. This people-level route overlaps the preserved Delaware (Lenape) entry; both labels remain available. Individual governments and language communities need their own specifically supported identities.

Read the sources [1] Delaware Tribe of Indians [2] Delaware Nation

03

Reading the Walking Purchase critically

Jennings examines the 1737 Walking Purchase through land papers and competing testimony. He argues that proprietary manipulation affected both dispossession and the records used to describe it. Read this as an attributed historical argument: the original manuscripts have not been independently checked here.

Read the sources [7] Pennsylvania History; facsimile hosted by Delaware Tribe of Indians

04

What the 1778 treaty actually says

The Fort Pitt treaty addresses peace, military passage, trade and territorial guarantees. Article VI proposes a state headed by the Delaware nation with congressional representation, expressly subject to congressional approval. A proposed arrangement is not proof that a state or seat was created. The document’s terms also do not demonstrate their fulfillment.

Read the sources [5] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database

05

A specifically scoped Texas connection

Delaware Nation connects its Absentee Delaware history with movement toward Texas and the Brazos reservation. Lipscomb’s Texas reference adds diplomacy, scouting and reserve-removal context. These accounts describe particular groups and stages; they do not place every Lenape community in Texas or establish all present families’ descent. Detailed migration and relocation chronology remains unfinished.

Read the sources [2] Delaware Nation [8] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas

06

An Ontario community’s own account

Eelünaapéewi Lahkéewiit’s Our Story follows a Moravian-connected community through displacement and rebuilding at Fairfield and New Fairfield. This is an Ontario community’s retrospective, distinct from the Oklahoma government also called Delaware Nation. Its wider historical claims and battle interpretation require comparison rather than automatic adoption.

Read the sources [6] Eelünaapéewi Lahkéewiit / Delaware Nation at Moraviantown

07

Learning through the Talking Dictionary

The Lenape Talking Dictionary identifies its main language scope as Southern Unami. Its introductory lesson explains spelling and everyday greetings, while documentation identifies speakers and other contributors. Selected entry text was read; audio playback was not tested. This resource does not stand for every Lenape language variety, and recordings retain their individual provenance.

Read the sources [3] Lenape Language Project / Delaware Tribe of Indians

08

Language programs in a dated account

Writing in 2002, Rementer and Pearson describe several generations of Oklahoma language classes, learning materials and the early dictionary project. Their different community relationships are explicit. The paper is useful program history, not a current speaker census or proof of learning outcomes. Language loss must not be read as disappearance of a people.

Read the sources [4] Delaware Tribe of Indians, hosting an authored paper

09

Reading path and remaining work

Start with community accounts, compare the treaty’s actual terms, and use the language resources within their stated scope. Jennings provides a focused example of archival criticism. This is a reviewed first reading foundation. Texas primary records, broader community perspectives and later histories still need substantial work; no completion or community endorsement is claimed.
